summary: Young children (ages ~5–6) learn to compose simple shapes into larger ones — two triangles into a rectangle or a bigger triangle, pattern blocks into a hexagon, basic shapes into a picture. The deep idea is PART–WHOLE: separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity. The Clements & Sarama composition trajectory describes growth from a Piece Assembler (each shape a separate part, trial and error), through a Picture Maker (combines pieces but does NOT anticipate the new shape, matches side lengths not angles), to a Shape Composer (anticipates the fit — 'I know what will fit' — using angles and intentional rotation/flip). The core vehicle is a graded sequence of pattern-block and tangram puzzles moving from fully-outlined to open, pitched about one trajectory level above the child's current one, supported by physical blocks and cut-out triangles.
misconceptions: Places shapes separately or by pure trial and error, not anticipating that pieces will combine into a new shape.
Matches side LENGTHS but not ANGLES, so pieces leave gaps/overlaps or a corner won't fit the space (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).
Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.
Sees the result as still 'two triangles' rather than one new rectangle — misses the part-whole identity of the composite.

activities.title: Two triangles become one rectangle
steps: Take two identical right triangles (physical cut-outs and/or an on-screen pair beside a rectangle outline).
Before moving them, answer the prompt 'What ONE shape do you think these will make?'
Arrange them to fill a rectangle outline, turning one triangle (if both start facing the same way, about 180°) so the corners and edges meet with no gaps or overlaps.
Rearrange the same two triangles to make a LARGER triangle by joining matching legs; unless the triangles are isosceles right triangles, you will need to flip one over, not just turn it.
Say aloud what single shape you have made each time: 'I put two triangles together and made one rectangle.'
activities.insight: Two separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity (part–whole); the same two pieces can compose into different wholes depending on how they are turned, flipped and joined.

activities.title: Fill the hexagon — graded puzzles from outlined to open
steps: Fill a hexagon with pattern blocks, starting from a fully-outlined puzzle (each block's place shown) and progressing toward an open outline (only the overall hexagon shown).
Before each placement, answer 'What will fit here, and why?'
Find at least two different ways to fill the same hexagon (e.g. two trapezoids; six triangles; a trapezoid plus three triangles).
Check the finished fill for any gaps or overlaps and fix them.
activities.insight: A whole shape can be composed in more than one way, and a correct fit depends on both side length and the angle of the space being filled.

activities.title: Turning a piece to make it fit
steps: Meet a gap that a square or triangle would fill only when it is rotated off its horizontal base.
First try a matched puzzle where the same piece fits with a horizontal base, then return to the rotated version.
Physically turn the cut-out piece (or rotate the on-screen piece) and watch that turning does not change what the shape is.
Seat the piece once its corner matches the corner of the gap.
activities.insight: A shape keeps its identity when rotated; turning a piece is a tool for making its corner match the space it must fill.

activities.title: Make a picture from basic shapes
steps: Use tangrams or pattern blocks to compose a picture or design (e.g. a house, a rocket, an animal) from basic shapes.
Explain which smaller shapes make up one part of the picture.
Where two pieces together form a familiar larger shape, name that larger shape.
activities.insight: Everyday pictures and designs are built by combining basic shapes, and the same basic shapes can be put together in many different ways.

checkQuestion: Set two tasks and watch how the child works: (1) Give two identical right triangles — 'Can you put these two triangles together to make a rectangle? Now can you make a bigger triangle?' (2) Give pattern blocks and a hexagon outline — 'Fill this hexagon exactly with these blocks.'
checkAnswer: (1) Places the two right triangles together (rotating one) to form a rectangle, and re-arranges them to form a larger triangle, recognising each result as a new single shape. (2) Fills the hexagon exactly — e.g. two trapezoids, or six triangles, or a trapezoid plus three triangles — with no gaps or overlaps, rotating pieces as needed.
